title: Procedure: your first project, click by click
prompt: How do I start my first project, step by step?
summary: Create the project, send a well-formed description ending with the Blueprint request, accept defaults one at a time, approve the Blueprint, confirm Local defaults, then follow the next-step chip through the four work products to Start build.

items.title: 1 Projects panel: Create
items.detail: Name the project after the application. A bounded session (chat) opens for it.

items.title: 2 Send the description
items.detail: Include people, current situation, desired improvement, fields, rules, examples, then Scope: Local Development only. Finalize discovery from this description and generate the Discovery Blueprint for review. Do not design or build yet.

items.title: 3 Accept measurable defaults
items.detail: Option cards disable the composer until you answer. Click the recommended option, or the card's Answer button to write your own words.

items.title: 4 Approve the Discovery Blueprint
items.detail: Review entity, fields, states, roles, floorplans and topology recommendation; approve.

items.title: 5 Confirm the landscape
items.detail: Click Use Local defaults and confirm in the nudge above the conversation.

items.title: 6 Work products
items.detail: Click the next-step chip in the composer four times, approving each card: Requirements, Delivery Plan, Solution Design, Build Plan.

items.title: 7 Start build.
items.detail: Send exactly Start build. and watch the progress. Then accept the Business Review and click Open in EAL.

blocks.text: Keep the composer for corrections and commands; use the cards for answers. If the composer says Respond to the interaction above, a card is waiting.

title: Procedure: writing a first prompt that converges in one turn
prompt: How should I phrase my first prompt so discovery converges quickly?
summary: Describe the app the way a colleague would: who, current state, desired change, fields, rules with examples, who sees which records, scope, and the closing instruction to generate the Blueprint. Pre-answer the usual questions.

blocks.caption: Seven parts, three to eight sentences in total.

blocks.title: A prompt that converged in one turn
blocks.before: We track mileage claims in a spreadsheet. Employees email trips; managers cannot see what is approved.
blocks.after: Build a Mileage Reimbursement Log. Employees log trips (date, from, to, miles, rate per mile); the app computes amount = miles x rate rounded half-up to 2 decimals. Managers approve or reject; employees see only their own claims, managers see their team. The name field is not tied to identity. Scope: Local Development only. Finalize discovery from this description and generate the Discovery Blueprint for review. Do not design or build yet.

rows: State business facts as the requesting user
I confirm the topology / architecture (authority conflict; discovery oscillates)
Accept 2 to 5 default cards one at a time
Apply all defaults without asking (per-turn model-call cap)
Leaving the rule for later and correcting at Build Plan
Say the UI, API, DB split is a recommendation
Confirming technical topology as a fact
Asking to build in the first message

plPrompts.label: Use the mileage prompt as a template

Managers approve or reject; employees see only their own claims, managers see their team. The name field is not tied to identity. Scope: Local Development only. Finalize discovery from this description and generate the Discovery Blueprint for review. Do not design or build yet.

title: Procedure: answering PL's questions and option cards
prompt: How do I answer PL's questions and options?
summary: Click the recommended option to accept a measurable default; use the card's Answer button to write your own words; the composer is disabled while a card waits; defects such as Insufficient dimensions mean more discovery is needed.

blocks.title: Interaction card
fields: Or answer in your own words

items.title: Read the question and its options
items.detail: The recommended option is a measurable default: a number, a rule or a visibility choice you can verify later.

items.title: Click an option
items.detail: The answer is recorded as your decision with your authority; the composer re-enables.

items.title: Or answer in your own words
items.detail: Click Answer on the card, type in Or answer in your own words, click Answer. Free text in the main composer is not accepted while a card waits.

items.title: If PL says Insufficient dimensions
items.detail: Discovery has not covered enough: add the missing facts (actors, process, data, rules) in your next message.

items.title: If an UNSUPPORTED_CONFIRMED defect appears
items.detail: Restate the fact plainly as the requesting user (We round to two decimals) instead of confirming a technical assumption.

title: Procedure: the exact commands that move a project forward
prompt: Which exact commands move the project forward?
summary: Lifecycle commands continue the active revision. The next-step chip in the composer always carries the right one; typing a capability-style request instead opens a new business revision.

rows: ... Finalize discovery from this description and generate the Discovery Blueprint for review. Do not design or build yet.
Create the Requirements for the current app from the approved Discovery Blueprint. Show it for review. Do not build or create files yet.
Create the Delivery Plan for the current app from the approved Requirements. Show it for review. Do not build or create files yet.
Create the Solution Design for the current app from the approved Delivery Plan. Show it for review. Do not build or create files yet.
Create the Build Plan for the current app from the approved Solution Design. Show it for review. Do not build or create files yet.
Show the Business Review for the current release.
Add ... to the current application and show the impact of the change for review. Do not build or create files yet.

blocks.caption: Order matters: each command consumes the approved head before it.

blocks.text: Approving a new version of Requirements or the Delivery Plan supersedes everything after it. Regenerate in this order; do not jump ahead.

title: Procedure: approving, requesting changes and the cascade
prompt: How do approvals and Request change work?
summary: Each work product card has Approve and Request change. Approving records a typed decision; Request change stores a rejection and asks for the correction; content is fixed by regenerating the earliest affected work product, usually Requirements.

rows.label: Approve
rows.value: Records your decision on this version; the next-step chip advances.

rows.label: Request change
rows.value: Your text is stored as a rejection effect on that version. It does not edit the content. Send the correction as a Requirements change so the cascade carries it downstream.

rows.label: Cascade
rows.value: New Requirements or Delivery Plan versions supersede their dependents. Delivery Plan, Solution Design and Build Plan regenerate in order from canonical inputs.

rows.label: Iteration budget
rows.value: Each regeneration spends several workflow iterations; at most one review round per work product fits comfortably, so put the whole correction in one message.

title: Procedure: when Start build is eligible and what to do when it is refused
prompt: When is Start build eligible and what if it is refused?
summary: Eligible when Requirements, Delivery Plan, Solution Design and Build Plan heads all belong to the active revision and the session has enough budget. Refusals name the missing item; a failed session accepts Start build again.

rows: All four work products approved on the current revision
Regenerate the missing one with its lifecycle command
First build needs an approved Discovery Blueprint
At least 181k tokens remaining of the 750k ceiling
Roll over to the successor chat
Answer with an explicit full-stack sentence; do not restate requirements

blocks.text: A session in failed state still accepts a new Start build. after the cause is fixed; its status returns to understanding and the build resumes with the same approvals.

title: Procedure: session budgets and rolling over to a successor chat
prompt: What are session budgets and rollover?
summary: Each chat has a 750k-token ceiling; a full-stack build needs at least 181k remaining. When PL reports WORKFLOW_STEP_TOKEN_RESERVATION_UNAVAILABLE, roll over: a successor chat in the same project carries approvals, landscape and knowledge forward.

items.label: Chat 1
items.detail: Discovery, Blueprint, work products: budget spent on understanding and drafting

items.label: Budget check
items.detail: Start build needs 181k; 138k left

items.label: Successor chat
items.detail: Same project; approvals and knowledge carried forward; fresh 750k

items.label: Start build.
items.detail: Runs in the successor

rows.label: Why budgets exist
rows.value: Model calls are metered per turn and per session so a runaway conversation cannot spend without limit.

rows.label: Per-turn cap
rows.value: A small number of model calls per turn; asking for many things at once hits MODEL_CALL_LIMIT_EXCEEDED.

rows.label: Rollover
rows.value: The project offers a successor primary chat; nothing is lost. The composer shows the rollover command when the budget is low.

title: Procedure: revisions, and why a new one sometimes opens
prompt: What is a revision and why did a new one open?
summary: A business revision is one coherent version of the application's intent. Lifecycle commands stay on the active revision; capability-style requests (Build me ..., Create an app that ...) open a new one, which resets first-build eligibility.

rows: Create the Requirements for the current app from the approved Blueprint ...
Build me a ... / Create an app that ...
Add a field to the current application and show the impact
Evolution on the active application, after release

blocks.text: Use the next-step chip. It always carries the lifecycle wording for the active revision.

title: Procedure: reading and accepting the Business Review
prompt: How do I review and accept a release?
summary: The Business Review lists checks with results and evidence observed in a real browser against the running application. Accept to activate the release in EAL; reject with a reason to record a rejection and return to Requirements.

items.title: Read the check table
items.detail: Each row is a requirement-derived check: pass, blocked (a rule correctly refused something) or fail, with the observed evidence.

items.title: Compare with your Requirements
items.detail: If a rule you care about is missing, reject and add it to Requirements; do not accept and hope.

items.title: Accept
items.detail: Records your acceptance as a typed event; the release is activated in EAL and roles are published to UME.

items.title: Open in EAL
items.detail: Sign in with the test identity PL created and create the first record.

plPrompts.label: Ask for the Business Review
plPrompts.prompt: Show the Business Review for the current release.

title: Procedure: opening your application in EAL
prompt: How do I open my app in EAL and sign in?
summary: After acceptance, click Open in EAL. Sign in as the test identity pl.app-name.user (or a UME user with the app's role), pick the application, and use the chat or the full view. Forms are registered tasks; confirm writes explicitly.

rows.label: Chat
rows.value: Type the registered task phrase (for example Create a mileage log record.), fill the form, then click Send and confirm. Enter alone is unreliable.

rows.label: Full view
rows.value: The generated UI (worklist, form) opened by EAL with a signed authority; the API resolves your roles live.

rows.label: Roles
rows.value: Published to UME at release; managers and submitters see different records exactly as the Blueprint's role matrix said.

rows.label: Forms
rows.value: Registered forms are controlled: set each field, confirm; the API rejects invalid values with VALIDATION_FAILED and writes nothing.

title: EAL: the runtime where AI-native applications are used
prompt: What is EAL and what is it used for?
summary: EAL, the Enterprise AI Launchpad, is the runtime loop of the platform. Users sign in, find their applications, chat with registered tasks, fill confirmed forms, approve human tasks and open the full UI. PL builds and releases; EAL runs. Roles come from UME; every write is confirmed and receipted.
takeaways: EAL is where business users live; PL is where applications are made.
Everything a user can do in EAL is a registered task or form published by the application's release.
Writes are confirmed by the user and receipted by the application; nothing happens silently.

rows: Signs in once; sees the applications assigned to their roles
UME resolves principals, roles and effective access
Types a registered task phrase, for example Create a mileage log record.
Deterministic routing to the registered task; the app API is called with signed authority
Completes the registered form, reviews, confirms
Field values are synchronised; the API validates and writes with an idempotency receipt
Claims, approves, rejects, delegates human tasks
Human-workflow state machine with role checks; password step-up for sensitive actions
Launches the generated UI (worklist, form, timeline)
EAL passes a signed authority reference; the API resolves it live
Previews assignments, sets retention and legal holds, exports privacy data

layers.title: Release hand-off
items: Signed release set to the EAL registry

layers.title: EAL (runtime loop)
items: Full view of the generated UI

rows: Deterministic task routing over registered tasks
Approvals on work products and builds
Signed application authority per request; confirmed writes

plPrompts.label: Ask PL about EAL
plPrompts.prompt: What is EAL and what is it used for? Explain how it differs from this chat and what a business user does there. Do not build anything.

title: Procedure: seeing what PL understood, decided and still needs
prompt: Where do I see what PL understood and decided?
summary: The Knowledge Inspector above the conversation shows five views for the project: current state, decision register, assumptions and risks, coverage gaps and source trace. It is the same ledger the model reads.

rows.label: Current state
rows.value: What PL believes about the application now: goal, actors, entity, process, topology.

rows.label: Decision register
rows.value: Every accepted default and approval, with who decided and when.

rows.label: Assumptions and risks
rows.value: What PL assumed to move fast, marked assumed, confirmed or corrected.

rows.label: Coverage gaps
rows.value: Discovery dimensions still open or deferred; Insufficient dimensions points here.

rows.label: Source trace
rows.value: Which message or artifact each item came from.

blocks.text: If PL seems to have forgotten something, check the source trace first; the message may have been a correction that was stored as a rejection rather than as content.

title: Procedure: messages you may see and what to do
prompt: Something went wrong. What do the common messages mean and what should I do?
summary: A short table of the messages new users meet most, what each means, and the exact next action.

rows: Discovery has not covered enough of actors, process, data or rules
Add the missing facts in one message; accept the default cards
You confirmed something as an authority you do not hold (topology, architecture)
Restate business facts as the requesting user; call the UI/API/DB split a recommendation
Too many model calls in one turn
Ask for one thing per turn; accept defaults one card at a time
Session budget too low for the build
Roll over to the successor chat, then Start build.
A work product was regenerated too many times
Put the whole correction in one Requirements change; approve once
A card is waiting for your answer
A head is missing on the active revision
Accept the recovery PL proposes; never edit files
The model provider refused or throttled
Wait and retry; PL retries automatically for a few minutes

title: The nine screen shapes PL can generate
prompt: What kinds of screens can PL generate?
summary: Worklist, object page, business form, calendar workspace, overview, review and decision, guided task, analytical list and case timeline. The Blueprint binds one or two of them; the compiler generates the React UI.

rows: Lists people work from, with filters and status
One record with sections and related items
Create or edit one record with validation
Chronology of a case with actions

plPrompts.label: Ask PL to propose screens
plPrompts.prompt: Based on the accepted users and workflow, propose the screens this application needs, name the floorplan for each, and mark open questions. Do not build files.

title: The capabilities installed in your workspace
prompt: Which capabilities are installed in my workspace?
summary: The list below comes from the running platform, not from this guide. Installed means PL can route to it; execution still depends on inputs, approvals and environment.

blocks.intro: These are the capabilities registered in the PL instance you are signed in to. A capability that is not installed is described but cannot be used from this chat.

blocks.caption: Every message is understood, routed to one capability and executed as bounded workflow steps.

blocks.text: Installed capability names are not a promise of execution readiness. PL checks permissions, inputs and environments when work is requested.

plPrompts.label: Ask PL for its capabilities
plPrompts.prompt: Show the main capabilities available in this workspace. Distinguish what is installed, what needs configuration or approval, and what is unavailable. Do not perform any build or deployment.
